claim_en: Axel Olof Freudenthal promoted racial doctrines holding that the Swedish-speaking upper class belonged to a Swedish master race while Finns were an inferior, dim-witted, and barbaric Turanian race incapable of creating culture independently.

Axel Olof Freudenthal's views on Finnish speakers were negative and based on 19th-century racial ideas, while unsourced claims framing modern Swedish People's Party awards and language policy as 'Freudenthalist racism' should be omitted or marked disputed.
Finnish nationalists opposed racial oppression everywhere and rejected racial theories.
A declaration by the Association of Finnish Culture and Identity proves that Enestam's accusations of fascism were completely unfounded.

Svecomania did not completely die out, and the radical views of contemporary activists like Ida Asplund regarding relations between Swedish-speaking Finns and the linguistic majority can be considered remnants of it.
Swedish-controlled media and Swedish financial power deliberately smear the Association of Finnish Culture and Identity and suppress discussion of the privileges of Swedish-speakers in Finland.
Svecomania involved racism directed against Finnish-speakers.

Past criticism and funding controversies regarding Suomalaisuuden Liitto are outdated or irrelevant, and the organisation focuses on non-discriminatory cultural preservation and selling flag products rather than anti-Swedish bigotry or anti-immigration.
Svecomania involved racism towards Finnish-speakers.

Following parliamentary written questions accusing the Association of Finnish Culture and Identity of ethnic agitation, the Finnish Government concluded that the association had committed no crime, while broader criticism of the association stems from its leadership's radical statements and activities rather than its program alone.

The contemporary equivalent of a Svecoman is a 'pakkoruotsittaja' (enforcer of mandatory Swedish), a label applying to politicians such as Tarja Halonen, Paavo Lipponen, and Johannes Virolainen who allegedly pushed through mandatory Swedish education and language laws over quality teaching, impact assessments, and expert opinions.

In 18th-century Sweden, isolated proposals were made to assimilate Finnish commoners and eradicate the Finnish language without leading to action, while monolingual Swedish-speaking officials' lack of Finnish skills was frequently seen as a problem despite state promises to consider language skills in appointments.
Swedish-language surnames borne by Finnish-speaking people were not objectively imposed by a Swedish occupation power, though Pentti Huttunen regarded them as forcibly imposed.

Svecomania has not completely disappeared, as the Swedish People's Party still honors Axel Olof Freudenthal as a spiritual father with medals named after him, and contemporary activists continue the tradition.
18th-century Fennophile figures should be referred to by their established Swedish/Latinate names (such as Daniel rather than Taneli) without Finnish-language patronymic glosses.
Ruins of Russian fortifications in Åland exist in multiple locations, with Boxö island being one example.
Fennomania is closely related to general concepts of nationalism construction, such as invented traditions, imagined communities, statuomania, and cultural canons.
The Finnish Party was a predecessor of, and its members transitioned in 1918 into, the National Coalition Party under its historical name Kansallinen Kokoomuspuolue.

Today in Finland there are two registered associations named Suomalainen Puolue, one founded in Vantaa and another founded in Nivala in 2006 by former members of the Independence Party who split over participating in the 2009 European Parliament election.
In 2020, a youth action group called Uudenmaan akseli was founded under Suomen Sisu.

Proto-Sámi developed either from an early Proto-Finnic split across northern Fennoscandia or, according to linguist Ante Aikio, in a smaller area in southern Finland during the Pre-Roman Iron Age, and Finnish law defines Sámi status through self-identification combined with ancestral tax or electoral records.

The Sámi Parliament of Finland is controlled by descendants of 19th-century arrivals who systematically discriminate against Inari Sámi and Forest Sámi by excluding them from the electoral roll and denying their indigenous status.
Claims lacking citations should be omitted while previously hidden descriptions of saga traditions and al-Idrisi's account should be visible in the article.
The Sámi differ greatly in ethnic origin from Baltic Finns, as evidenced primarily by their small stature and distinct facial features.
Forest Sámi are an established Sámi group in Finland with their own language, Kemi Sámi, which is being revitalised rather than extinct.
Forest Sámi are reviving the Kemi Sámi language, starting with an upcoming Kemi Sámi ABC book.

The existence of 'Kuningas' as a personal name in medieval Finland does not preclude the existence of actual kings, just as 'King' exists as a surname in England despite England having had Iron Age monarchs.

Associating the term 'lappalaiset' with the Sámi belongs to the past, the term is derogatory when applied to the Sámi today, and it is uncertain whether historical mentions of 'lappalaiset' referred to Sámi ancestors at all.
The view that ancient Finnish kings were local clan or expedition leaders represents general current scholarly understanding rather than merely the opinion of archaeologist J.-P. Taavitsainen.
The Kemi Sámi (Forest Sámi) still exist today as a distinct people numbering approximately 5,000 to 15,000, with much of their culture preserved.
The historical definition of 'lappalaiset' as nomadic hunter-gatherers outside agricultural areas is merely an older conception, and another view in the article is controversial.

Three endangered Sámi languages—Northern, Inari, and Skolt Sámi—are spoken in Finland, and 75% of Sámi children under 10 live outside the Sámi homeland, while claims that Finns and Sámi are equally indigenous and recently differentiated should be omitted.

There are other state-recognized and self-declared indigenous peoples in Europe besides the Sámi, and the Sámi's status as an indigenous people with cultural autonomy is recognized in the Constitution of Finland.
Forest Sámi are an official or established Sámi group in Finland, and Kemi Sámi is still spoken by some people and only erroneously considered extinct.
Modern Finns derive most of their genetic ancestry from Central Europe and earlier Germanic inhabitants rather than from Finno-Ugric-speaking migrants from the Volga–Oka–Kama region.

Ancient DNA indicates that the ancestors of the Sámi probably formed the original population of Finland, and Sámi languages were spoken across the region before the arrival of the ancestors of modern Finns.
Forest Sámi have an ongoing revitalization project for their nearly extinct language and expect to publish a Kemi Sámi primer soon.
Western Finns are of Frankish descent, Franks inhabited Southwest Finland prior to Finns and named the Aura River after Franconian 'Aurach' rivers before adopting the Finnish language.

Finland did not exist as a historical concept prior to being artificially invented in the 19th century by Swedish-speaking elites, and there is no historical evidence for the existence of a Finnish people or identity.

Tacitus's description of the Fenni aligns with Finnish wilderness tradition and gender equality research, representing a narrow but accurate view formed by foreign fur traders visiting temporary seasonal trading posts.

An ancient language called "paleojärvimaa" (Palaeo-Lakelandic) was theorised to have been spoken in Finland, and ancient languages spoken in the region left traces in current place names as well as in Sámi and Finnish vocabularies.
The Sámi people settled the entirety of Northern Europe.
Sápmi is used as a primary name alongside Saamenmaa in Finnish, and the region encompasses Finnish Lapland, Northern Sweden, Central and Northern Norway, and Murmansk Oblast.

The Mesolithic Suomusjärvi, Kunda, and Swiderian cultures were already Finno-Ugric-speaking, meaning the linguistic ancestors of Finns arrived in Finland around 10,000 years ago immediately after the Ice Age.

Forest Sámi vocabulary survived into the 20th century and up to the present day among elders, large-scale reindeer herding is the youngest Sámi livelihood, and Forest Sámi became recorded as settler farmers in tax registers after turning to agriculture when hunting declined.
Karelians are traditionally identical to Lapps (lappalaiset).
Tacitus's description of the Fenni was long considered the first detailed description of the Finns, but according to modern consensus it refers to the Sámi.
Archaeology shows that no migrations to Finland took place, rendering the Volga bend homeland theory irrelevant and supported as possible only by a portion of linguists.
The archaeological dating of the Ristola and Orimattila sites is questionable, and a proposed 130,000–140,000-year timeline for dog domestication could push back the dating of Finno-Ugric peoples.

Materials from the Blue-and-Black Movement were found at the home of a minor who committed a racist stabbing in Oulu, an activist of the movement was arrested for carrying a knife, and various violent offenders as well as local politicians from other parties have signed its supporter cards.

The Finnish People First (SKE) party is nationalist and socioeconomically left-centrist rather than far-right, and since expelling Marco de Wit, chairwoman Riikka Salmi has steered it in a more humane direction.
The Finnish Resistance Movement should be described as National Socialist rather than neo-Nazi, as the latter term unfairly smears nationalists.
Historian Oula Silvennoinen has political commitments to the Green League that should be noted alongside his academic assessment of the Blue-and-Black Movement as fascist.
The Lapua Movement (or its leader Vihtori Kosola) is still highly respected in Lapua today.
Vihtori Kosola is still a highly respected man in Lapua.

A faction of the Finnish People First party leadership was declared illegal in court, its authorised signatories were replaced at the Patent and Registration Office and Ministry of Justice, and skepuolue.fi became the official party website.

During a September 2016 Finnish Resistance Movement demonstration at Helsinki's Asema-aukio, a man who intervened was knocked down onto his head due to provocation and died a week later of a cerebral hemorrhage after being discharged from the hospital.
The authors of a cited work on the Finnish far-right are left-wing radicals, and researcher Vesa Puuronen formerly belonged to the minority communists.
A mole infiltrated the administration of the Rajat kiinni! group in October 2016 to delete members, and certain critical characterisations of the movement are merely matters of opinion or erroneous.

Twelve out of the Blue-and-Black Movement's 88 parliamentary election candidates in 2023 had criminal convictions for various offenses including assault, attempted manslaughter, ethnic agitation, drug crimes, and firearms offenses.

Ano Turtiainen stated that Molotov cocktail attacks on reception centres are important elimination tasks that should next target the Finnish Red Cross, a Facebook comment liked by MP Laura Huhtasaari, without describing him as an 'immigration critic'.
Timo Soini is politically independent as of June 16, 2017, having been expelled from the Finns Party after being a member from 1995 to 2017.

At the Helsinki Railway Square demonstration, a passerby spat toward a Finnish Resistance Movement member and argued with him, prompting a participant to kick the departing man to the ground in retaliation for his disrespectful behaviour.
Marco de Wit is the leader of the Suomen Kansa Ensin association and previously participated in both the Suomi Ensin and Rajat kiinni! civic movements.
The definition of the far right as radical political right-wing movements (or right-wing radicalism) stems from Marxist terminology.
Ano Turtiainen is a long-time entrepreneur, odd-job man, and the permanent leader of the Power Belongs to the People party.
Ano Turtiainen has never received a competition ban in sports, contrary to news reports by STT and Helsingin Sanomat.

In April 2005 Alexander Stubb proposed holding EU meetings in English and French, and at the start of Finland's EU presidency he did not arrange German interpretation, prompting Germany to boycott a ministerial meeting in June 2006.
The Finnish Resistance Movement has a racist agenda.
Demonstrations by the Nordic Resistance Movement in Finland are typically peaceful and only become violent due to deliberate provocation by outsiders.

A Suomi Ensin activist was arrested on June 11 for brandishing a handgun in central Helsinki, and police are investigating the movement's activists for maintaining an illegal registry of political opponents such as anti-fascists.
Populism is not a political party line or program, but rather an activity aimed at gaining popularity, making it a means rather than a goal.

The Patriotic People's Movement (IKL) should not be characterized in the lead as a far-right party heavily influenced by German National Socialism and European fascism or as wearing Nazi-like swastika armbands.

Vihtori Kosola was the driving force of the Lapua Movement rather than merely its figurehead, whereas in the Patriotic People's Movement (IKL) he was a charismatic figurehead while Vilho Annala was the true leader.

Sinimusta Liike's ideology includes ethnonationalism and anti-Russian sentiment, and chairperson Tuukka Kuru stated that the party program was shortened for the Party Register mainly due to its length rather than its clauses.
Members of the Suomi Ensin movement filmed an asylum seeker's suicide attempt on March 8, 2017, while laughing, rejoicing, and shouting 'die' at the victim.

Despite fierce pressure from Finnish communists, the banned Patriotic People's Movement's property was not confiscated, and the proceeds from winding down its businesses were used in 1953 to establish the Foundation for the History of Finland in the 1920s–1940s.

In 2016, the Rajat Kiinni! movement protested against mainstream media, left-wing violence, and the Peli Poikki demonstration attended by society's elite, resulting in arrests and profanity-filled speeches.
One of the leading figures of the Suomi Ensin movement was arrested on suspicion of rape at a demonstration in Helsinki in September 2017.
On 16 February, police ordered demonstrations at Kiasma and Lasipalatsi to relocate, and after Suomi Ensin protesters disobeyed the order, police removed eight individuals and detained two.
Some contemporaries wanted Vihtori Kosola to become a fascist-style dictator of Finland, rather than merely suspecting or perceiving that such plans existed.

The Rajat kiinni! movement began in Salo on August 30, 2015, at a demonstration organized by Jani Salomaa where the phrase was first used, and claims that it began at later demonstrations in September 2015 are false.

In summer 1935, police confiscated 56 copies of the Sinimusta magazine in Helsinki and charged it with incitement against the state order, prompted at least by Elias Simojoki's May 31, 1935 article 'Luo lippujen' which mentioned a 'final solution'.

Suomi Ensin chairperson Mario Argenta publicly distanced himself from demonstrations, registering as a party, and supporting MV-lehti and Ilja Janitskin in the 2018 presidential election, considering these actions unilateral moves by Marco de Wit.
Ano Turtiainen has published numerous pro-Russian statements on Twitter since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, including demanding the lifting of sanctions against Russia.

The name Viena derives from the Russian river name (Severnaya) Dvina, and Ladoga Karelia corresponds to the modern Russian region of Northern Priladozhye (comprising only Lahdenpohja and Sortavala districts) and can be called 'Pohjois-Laatokkala' or 'Laatokkainen' in Finnish.

Before Swedish rule, a traditional 'Kalevala faith' and poetry existed in southern Finland, which Swedish authorities banned and forced underground, causing it to retreat to eastern Finland and Border Karelia.
Kalevala poetry originated in southern Finland (Tavastia) and shifted eastward to Border Karelia during Swedish rule due to 16th–17th century witch trials and church orthodoxy.

The view that Kalevala poems were solely Karelian enabled Svecomans to disparage Finnish-speakers' poetic abilities, whereas the poems actually had a Finnish or Western Finnish origin, supported by Agricola listing Väinämöinen, Ilmarinen, and Ahti as Tavastian rather than Karelian gods.
White Karelia is also called 'Belaja Karelija' and abbreviated 'Belomorje' in Russian, and bears the same name in Karelian as in Finnish.

Archaeological evidence of a 1150s pagan reaction in the Nousiainen region suggests that the killing of Bishop Henry stemmed from broader regional socio-political currents rather than solely the reaction of Lalli and his wife.

Following the Swedish conquest in the 1250s, old Finnish chieftains were executed and replaced by loyalists called 'munkkilaiset', while earlier settlers known as 'hiidet' were assimilated and non-Sámi 'lappalaiset' in Tavastia maintained witchcraft before disappearing or assimilating.
The White Sea Isthmus, Dvina Bay, and Northern Dvina river are closely related to the history and cultural sphere of White Karelia.
During the First Swedish Crusade in the 1150s, Swedes invaded pagan Finland to conquer land and spread Christianity, prompting Finns to rebel against paying church taxes.

White Karelia's historical subdivisions should be called parishes (pitäjät) rather than municipalities (kunnat), its Russian name can be shortened to Belaja Karelija / Belomorje, and the Muezersky and Segezha districts belong to Olonets Karelia rather than White Karelia.
18th-century Fennophile figures should be referred to by their established Swedish/Latinate names (such as Daniel rather than Taneli) without Finnish-language patronymic glosses.
The Russian name Belaja Karelija and the etymology of Viena from the Russian river name Dvina should not be included based on unreliable sources like wikis and blogs.

A pagan reaction in 12th-century Southwestern Finland would mean that the killing of Bishop Henry was driven by a broader societal reaction rather than merely the personal emotional outbursts of Lalli and his wife.

The Kalevala is also part of history.
Lalli and Bishop Henry may be fictional rather than historical figures.
Bishop Henry was killed on the ice of Lake Köyliö by the peasant Lalli after Lalli's wife Kerttu lied that Henry had taken food without paying, and the crusade took place possibly in the 1150s.
The poems of the Kalevala have retained their place in Finland to this day.
Bishop Henry died on Lake Köyliönjärvi as a result of a blow to the head from Lalli's axe.
